title: BioBlobs: Unsupervised Discovery of Functional Substructures
claim: A learned encoder, partitioner and predictor chain compresses an input into a few compact, weighted parts that drive the final prediction.
layout: 2 rows: top left-to-right pipeline, bottom two dashed zoom-in panels
description: The figure has a top row that reads left to right. A protein sequence string and a blue 3D cartoon structure feed a light-blue 'Protein Encoder' box. Its output is a residue graph with colored embedding bars. That graph feeds an orange 'BLOB Neural Partitioner' box, which splits into stacked gray boxes 'Blob 1' to 'Blob K', and these go to a green 'BLOB MIL Predictor' box. Dashed orange and green lines connect the two modules to zoom-in panels below. The left panel shows seed selection, then blob expansion with proximity weights, and an L_Hoyer sparsity feedback loop. The right panel shows blob membership pooling, then linear layers and attention gates giving blob embeddings and importance scores. Weighted pooling and a classifier follow. Color-coded boxes guide the eye.
caption: \textbf{The \tool{} pipeline.} A protein encoder maps the protein to residue embeddings. The neural blob partitioner selects $K$ seed residues and expands each into a blob within radius $r$, and the Hoyer-Square penalty keeps the blobs compact. The MIL predictor pools the residue embeddings of each blob, weights the blobs by their importance scores $\alpha_k$ and classifies the protein.
abstract: Protein function is often localized to cohesive substructures, such as catalytic triads, binding pockets, and structural motifs, that occupy only a small fraction of a protein's residues. Yet existing predictive pipelines typically aggregate residue-level embeddings and do not explicitly model or infer these functional substructures, leaving the central biological question unanswered: which substructure of a protein is responsible for its function? We introduce BioBlobs, an encoder-agnostic, end-to-end differentiable framework that compresses a protein into a small set of cohesive substructures (blobs) and predicts function from these blobs alone, so that each blob corresponds to a candidate functional region. Across diverse protein function prediction tasks and both sequence-only and structure-aware protein language models, BioBlobs is competitive with strong baselines while operating on only a small fraction of residues. Trained only on protein function labels, BioBlobs recovers expert-curated functional sites in InterPro and experimentally annotated catalytic sites in the Mechanism and Catalytic Site Atlas, demonstrating unsupervised functional substructure discovery and opening a path to large-scale functional site discovery in unannotated proteins. The discovered blobs adapt their spatial scale to the task, ranging from local catalytic sites to entire structural domains. Code is available at https://github.com/OliverLaboratory/BioBlobs.
